questions.title: How exactly does the partition function cancel out in the DPO derivation?
questions.question_body: In the DPO paper, they start from the KL-regularized objective and note that the optimal policy has the form $\pi_r(y\mid x) \propto \pi_{\text{ref}}(y\mid x)\exp\left(\tfrac{1}{\beta} r(x,y)\right)$. They then plug this into the Bradley–Terry model so that the partition function $Z(x)$ cancels, yielding a preference probability that depends only on $\log \tfrac{\pi^*(y\mid x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y\mid x)}$. Could someone show the algebra step-by-step for the cancellation, starting from $p(y_1 \succ y_2\mid x)=\sigma\big(r(x,y_1)-r(x,y_2)\big)$ and using $r(x,y)=\beta \log\tfrac{\pi^*(y\mid x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y\mid x)} + \beta\log Z(x)$?

questions.title: What is the precise relationship between the DPO temperature parameter $\beta$ and the achieved KL divergence?
questions.question_body: The DPO loss uses a hyperparameter $\beta$ that conceptually trades off reward maximization against staying close to $\pi_{\text{ref}}$. Is there a formal monotonic relationship between $\beta$ and the expected KL $\mathbb{E}[\mathbb{D}_{\mathrm{KL}}(\pi_\theta\Vert \pi_{\text{ref}})]$ under the optimal solution? In other words, if I decrease $\beta$, should I always expect the trained policy to have lower KL to $\pi_{\text{ref}}$? Can this be derived from the dual of the KL-constrained optimization or via Lagrange multipliers?

questions.title: What happens in the limits $\beta \to 0$ and $\beta \to \infty$ for DPO?
questions.question_body: Using the reparameterization $r(x,y)=\beta \log \tfrac{\pi(y\mid x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y\mid x)} + \beta\log Z(x)$, I am trying to build intuition for extreme values of $\beta$. As $\beta\to 0$, does DPO force $\pi$ to collapse to $\pi_{\text{ref}}$ regardless of preferences? As $\beta\to \infty$, does DPO effectively ignore the KL regularization and behave like maximizing a Bradley–Terry likelihood purely on $\log \pi(y\mid x)$ (up to length effects)? Are there stability issues in these limits?

questions.title: Should DPO use sequence-level or length-normalized log probabilities to avoid length bias?
questions.question_body: The DPO loss compares $\log \tfrac{\pi(y\mid x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y\mid x)}$ across a preferred $y_w$ and a dispreferred $y_l$. In an autoregressive LM, $\log \pi(y\mid x)$ is a sum over tokens, so longer sequences typically have lower log-prob. Does DPO use raw sequence log-probabilities (sum), per-token averages, or any explicit length normalization? How does this choice affect bias toward shorter or longer responses, especially in tasks like summarization?

questions.title: How justified is fitting $\pi_{\text{ref}}$ by maximum likelihood on preferred completions when the true SFT policy is unavailable?
questions.question_body: The paper suggests that when the original SFT policy $\pi^{\text{SFT}}$ used to sample preferences is unavailable, we can estimate a reference policy $\pi_{\text{ref}}$ by maximizing likelihood on the preferred completions $(x,y_w)$. Is this consistent under the DPO theory? What bias is introduced if the true data-generating policy differed significantly and the dataset contains only pairwise preferences but not a full distribution over $y$?

questions.title: How does DPO handle support mismatch when $\pi_{\text{ref}}(y\mid x)=0$ for some observed $y$?
questions.question_body: Since DPO relies on $\log \tfrac{\pi(y\mid x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y\mid x)}$, what happens if the reference model assigns zero (or numerically tiny) probability mass to an observed completion $y$ present in the preference dataset? Are there standard smoothing or floor-probability tricks to prevent exploding terms, and do these tricks affect the theoretical guarantees?

questions.title: Why does the DPO gradient weighting with $\sigma(\hat r(y_l)-\hat r(y_w))$ help avoid degeneracy compared to unlikelihood training?
questions.question_body: The paper claims that weighting each update by $\sigma(\hat r(y_l)-\hat r(y_w))$ prevents degeneration observed with a naive unlikelihood objective that only increases $\log \pi(y_w)$ and decreases $\log \pi(y_l)$. Can someone provide an intuitive and/or formal explanation for why this logistic weight stabilizes training? Is it because the weight downscales examples already well-ordered by the implicit reward $\hat r$, thus preventing runaway updates?

questions.title: Under what assumptions is DPO statistically consistent with Bradley–Terry preference data?
questions.question_body: The paper mentions that DPO enjoys consistency properties under the Bradley–Terry model. What are the exact assumptions (e.g., well-specified BT model, identifiability up to an additive function of $x$, sufficient support, no severe selection bias)? How do annotator noise, systematic label biases, or adversarial preferences affect consistency of the learned $\pi_\theta$?

questions.title: How does DPO extend to Plackett–Luce with more than two items per query?
questions.question_body: For preference lists of size $k>2$, the Plackett–Luce model defines a probability over permutations. How does the DPO objective change when we have an ordered list $(y_{(1)},\dots,y_{(k)})$ rather than a binary comparison? Is the loss just the negative log-likelihood of the ordered list under reparameterized scores $\beta \log \tfrac{\pi(y\mid x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y\mid x)}$, and how is the gradient computed efficiently for large $k$?

questions.title: If DPO and PPO optimize the same KL-regularized objective, why does DPO empirically dominate PPO on the reward–KL frontier?
questions.question_body: The paper reports that DPO produces a more efficient reward–KL frontier than PPO, even when PPO has access to the ground-truth reward in the sentiment task. What explains this discrepancy if both methods target the same constrained objective? Is it variance reduction from avoiding sampling in the inner loop, absence of value-function estimation error, better credit assignment, or something else?

questions.title: How does the control-as-inference view lead to the objective with the normalization term $f(r,\pi_{\text{ref}},\beta)$?
questions.question_body: In the control-as-inference derivation, minimizing $\mathbb{D}_{\mathrm{KL}}[\pi_\theta(\cdot\mid x)\Vert \pi^*(\cdot\mid x)]$ yields an objective with a baseline-like term $-\beta\log \sum_y \pi_{\text{ref}}(y\mid x)\exp\big(\tfrac{1}{\beta} r_\phi(x,y)\big)$. Could someone derive this objective in detail and explain how this term functions as a soft value function and why dropping or poorly estimating it makes actor–critic training unstable?

questions.title: Does DPO need importance weighting if preference pairs were sampled from a policy different from $\pi_{\text{ref}}$?
questions.question_body: Suppose the preference dataset was collected with a policy $q(y\mid x)$ that differs from the chosen $\pi_{\text{ref}}$. Since the DPO likelihood includes $\log \tfrac{\pi(y\mid x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y\mid x)}$, is it theoretically necessary to perform any off-policy correction or importance weighting to account for the mismatch between $q$ and $\pi_{\text{ref}}$? If not, why is it safe to ignore?

questions.title: Is DPO equivalent to a form of contrastive learning or InfoNCE on policy logits?
questions.question_body: The DPO loss for a pair $(y_w,y_l)$ resembles a logistic regression on the difference of scores $\beta \big(\log \pi(y_w\mid x)-\log \pi(y_l\mid x)\big)$ plus the same difference for $\pi_{\text{ref}}$. Is there a direct connection to contrastive objectives like InfoNCE that compare positive and negative samples, with $\log \pi(\cdot\mid x)$ serving as energy scores? If so, what is the precise mapping and what insights does it give about temperature $\beta$ and negative sampling?

questions.title: Is the implicit reward $\hat r_\theta(x,y)=\beta\log \tfrac{\pi_\theta(y\mid x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y\mid x)}$ a reward or an advantage?
questions.question_body: Because the DPO reparameterization is defined up to an additive $x$-dependent constant, $\hat r_\theta$ looks like a shaped reward or an advantage-like quantity with baseline tied to $\pi_{\text{ref}}$. Can we interpret $\hat r_\theta$ as a soft advantage function? Under what conditions does it correspond to $A(x,y)=Q(x,y)-V(x)$ in the KL-regularized RL formulation?

questions.title: Can someone re-derive the optimal policy $\pi_r(y\mid x) \propto \pi_{\text{ref}}(y\mid x) e^{r(x,y)/\beta}$ from the KL-constrained objective?
questions.question_body: Starting from the objective $\max_{\pi} \mathbb{E}_{y\sim \pi(\cdot\mid x)}[r(x,y)] - \beta\,\mathbb{D}_{\mathrm{KL}}[\pi(\cdot\mid x)\Vert \pi_{\text{ref}}(\cdot\mid x)]$ for each fixed $x$, can someone show the steps using calculus of variations or Lagrange multipliers that produce the closed-form optimal policy $\pi_r(y\mid x) = \tfrac{1}{Z(x)}\pi_{\text{ref}}(y\mid x) e^{r(x,y)/\beta}$ and explain the role of $Z(x)$?

questions.title: Does DPO require enumerating the full action space, or is it purely offline on given $(x, y_w, y_l)$ pairs?
questions.question_body: The DPO loss only requires evaluating $\log \pi(y_w\mid x)$ and $\log \pi(y_l\mid x)$ for observed pairs. Does this mean training is entirely offline without sampling rollouts from $\pi_\theta$? Are there scenarios where enumerating or sampling additional $y$ would help (e.g., to reduce estimation bias), or is DPO optimally data-efficient given the pairwise dataset?

questions.title: How would DPO handle ties or indifference in preferences (i.e., $y_w$ equals $y_l$ or tie labels)?
questions.question_body: Some preference datasets include ties or 'no preference' labels. The Bradley–Terry model is binary-preference-based. Are there standard extensions of DPO to handle ties (e.g., Davidson model or Thurstone–Mosteller variants) such that the loss gracefully accounts for indifference? What would the DPO objective look like in that case?

questions.title: What prevents over-optimization (reward hacking) in DPO when the dataset of preferences is small or biased?
questions.question_body: Since DPO directly pushes $\log \tfrac{\pi(y_w\mid x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y_w\mid x)}$ up and $\log \tfrac{\pi(y_l\mid x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y_l\mid x)}$ down, could it overfit to spurious heuristics present in a small or biased preference dataset? Are there regularizers (e.g., additional KL to $\pi_{\text{ref}}$, entropy, data augmentation) or early stopping criteria that mitigate this without requiring reinforcement learning?

questions.title: How are temperature at inference and $\beta$ during training related in practice?
questions.question_body: The paper reports that win rate depends on the sampling temperature at inference, while $\beta$ governs the strength of the KL constraint during training. Is there any principled relationship between sampling temperature $\tau$ at test time and the training regularization $\beta$? For instance, does scaling logits by $1/\tau$ partially counteract the effect of the KL regularization imposed by small $\beta$?

questions.title: Why might DPO generalize out-of-distribution comparably to PPO even though it does not use extra unlabeled prompts?
questions.question_body: In the TL;DR to CNN/DailyMail transfer, DPO outperforms PPO despite not using additional unlabeled prompts during training that PPO might benefit from. What theoretical or empirical reasons could explain this? Is it because DPO avoids error compounding associated with on-policy exploration when the reward or value function is mis-specified?

questions.title: How is sequence-level KL computed for autoregressive models, and does this favor shorter outputs?
questions.question_body: The paper mentions computing sequence-level KL as the sum of per-timestep KLs. For completions $y=(y_1,\dots,y_T)$, this is $\sum_{t=1}^T \mathbb{D}_{\mathrm{KL}}\big(\pi(\cdot\mid x,y_{<t})\Vert \pi_{\text{ref}}(\cdot\mid x,y_{<t})\big)$. Does this introduce a length dependence that interacts with the DPO training objective? Should sequence KL be normalized by length when comparing policies with different typical output lengths?

questions.title: How sensitive is the implicit reward to the choice of $\pi_{\text{ref}}$, and does this hurt identifiability?
questions.question_body: The implicit reward is defined as $\hat r_\theta(x,y)=\beta \log \tfrac{\pi_\theta(y\mid x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y\mid x)}$. This means changing $\pi_{\text{ref}}$ will change the numeric values of $\hat r_\theta$, even if preferences are unchanged up to equivalence classes. Does this affect comparability across experiments or transfer between tasks? Is there a recommended calibration procedure for $\pi_{\text{ref}}$?

questions.title: Can we combine DPO with supervised fine-tuning in a single multi-task objective?
questions.question_body: If we have both instruction-following demonstrations and pairwise preferences, is there any downside to optimizing a combined loss $\mathcal{L}=\mathcal{L}_{\text{SFT}}+\lambda\,\mathcal{L}_{\text{DPO}}$? Would this be equivalent to changing the effective $\beta$ or does it introduce a qualitatively different regularization that can improve stability or sample efficiency?

questions.title: What happens if the annotator preference noise does not match the logistic link used by Bradley–Terry?
questions.question_body: Bradley–Terry assumes $p(y_w\succ y_l\mid x)=\sigma\big(r(x,y_w)-r(x,y_l)\big)$ with a fixed slope. If the true noise is heavier-tailed or the slope varies across prompts (heteroskedasticity), does DPO become biased? Could a generalized linear model with a learned temperature per-example or per-batch (e.g., $\sigma(\alpha_x\,\Delta r)$) be integrated into DPO without breaking the closed-form optimal policy connection?

questions.title: What are the computational bottlenecks of DPO and how do they compare to PPO?
questions.question_body: In practice, DPO requires two forward passes per pair $(x,y_w)$ and $(x,y_l)$ to compute $\log \pi(\cdot\mid x)$ and $\log \pi_{\text{ref}}(\cdot\mid x)$. Are there tricks like caching $\pi_{\text{ref}}$ logits, shared encoders, or low-rank adapters that substantially reduce compute and memory? How does total wall-clock time compare to PPO for a fixed number of preference pairs?

questions.title: How robust is DPO if the Bradley–Terry model is misspecified (e.g., Thurstone or context-dependent preferences)?
questions.question_body: If the true preference process is better modeled by Thurstone–Mosteller or exhibits context effects violating Luce's choice axiom, how does DPO behave? Are there known generalizations of the DPO derivation for other pairwise choice models that retain the partition-function cancellation and closed-form optimal policy connection?

questions.title: Is the DPO objective a tight surrogate or a lower bound on the original RLHF objective?
questions.question_body: Since DPO directly maximizes the likelihood of preferences under the reparameterized policy, is $\mathcal{L}_{\text{DPO}}$ a tight surrogate to the KL-regularized reward maximization objective, or can it be viewed as a lower bound akin to a variational objective? Under what conditions do their optima coincide?

questions.title: Can DPO be applied to continuous action spaces or non-text modalities without modification?
questions.question_body: The derivation seems general, relying on a density $\pi(y\mid x)$ relative to a reference $\pi_{\text{ref}}(y\mid x)$. For continuous actions (e.g., diffusion models for images or audio), do we need any special considerations to evaluate $\log \tfrac{\pi(y\mid x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y\mid x)}$ reliably? Are there known successful applications of DPO-like objectives to non-text generative models?

questions.title: How is the evaluation win rate with GPT-4 calibrated to human preferences, and what are the pitfalls?
questions.question_body: The paper uses GPT-4 to estimate win rates against baselines, with some human validation. How sensitive are these win rates to the GPT-4 prompting, temperature, and context windows? What are best practices to ensure GPT-4 judgments correlate with human preferences, and are there failure modes where GPT-4 systematically disagrees with humans despite prompt tuning?
